notes.definition: Sulfate ions (SO₄²⁻) in solution are identified by adding dilute hydrochloric acid followed by barium chloride solution. A white precipitate of barium sulfate shows that sulfate ions are present.
explanation: To test a solution for sulfate ions, put a small amount in a test tube and add a few drops of dilute hydrochloric acid. Then add a few drops of barium chloride solution. If sulfate ions are present, a white precipitate forms immediately. The precipitate is barium sulfate, BaSO₄, which is insoluble in water.

The hydrochloric acid is added first to remove any carbonate ions. Carbonate ions would react with barium ions to form barium carbonate, which is also a white precipitate, so without the acid a carbonate could be mistaken for a sulfate. The acid reacts with carbonate ions to form carbon dioxide, removing them. Hydrochloric acid can be used here (unlike in the halide test) because barium chloride already contains chloride ions, and chloride ions do not form a precipitate with barium ions. Sulfuric acid must never be used, because it contains sulfate ions and would always give a white precipitate.

The reaction can be shown by a full equation, such as Na₂SO₄(aq) + BaCl₂(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq) or CuSO₄(aq) + BaCl₂(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + CuCl₂(aq). In the ionic equation (Higher tier) only the ions that form the precipitate are shown: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s). The metal ion from the sulfate and the chloride ions from barium chloride are spectator ions, which is why every soluble sulfate gives the same result.

Barium chloride solution is toxic, so it should be handled carefully, using small volumes, eye protection and washing hands afterwards. The sulfate test is part of required practical 7, in which you combine tests for positive ions (flame tests and sodium hydroxide) with tests for negative ions (carbonate, halides and sulfate) to identify an unknown ionic compound.
keyFacts: Test: add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution.

The acid removes carbonate ions, which would form white barium carbonate.
Hydrochloric acid is fine here because chloride ions do not precipitate with barium.

keyTerms.definition: The negative ion SO₄²⁻, found in compounds such as copper sulfate and sodium sulfate.
BaCl₂, a soluble barium compound used as the reagent in the sulfate test; it is toxic.
BaSO₄, an insoluble white solid formed in a positive sulfate test.
A result that wrongly suggests a substance is present, for example a precipitate caused by carbonate rather than sulfate.
An ion present in a reaction mixture that does not take part in the reaction.

workedExamples.title: Identifying a sulfate
workedExamples.question: A blue solution gives a blue precipitate with sodium hydroxide, and a white precipitate with dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride. Name the compound.
steps: Blue precipitate with NaOH shows copper(II) ions.
White precipitate with acidified barium chloride shows sulfate ions.
Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ combine 1:1 as CuSO₄.

workedExamples.title: Writing the equation
workedExamples.question: Write a balanced equation for the reaction between magnesium sulfate solution and barium chloride solution, and the ionic equation.
steps: Swap partners: magnesium sulfate + barium chloride → barium sulfate + magnesium chloride.
MgSO₄(aq) + BaCl₂(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + MgCl₂(aq). Check: all atoms balance.
Remove the spectator ions Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻.
workedExamples.answer: MgSO₄(aq) + BaCl₂(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + MgCl₂(aq); Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s)

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say the precipitate in the sulfate test is barium chloride.
misconceptions.right: In fact barium chloride is the soluble reagent. The white precipitate is barium sulfate, BaSO₄.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often use sulfuric acid to acidify the sample.
misconceptions.right: In fact sulfuric acid contains sulfate ions, so it would always give a white precipitate. Use dilute hydrochloric acid.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the acid is not needed.
misconceptions.right: In fact carbonate ions would give a white precipitate of barium carbonate, so the acid is needed to remove them.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think hydrochloric acid cannot be used because it contains chloride, as in the halide test.
misconceptions.right: In fact chloride ions do not form a precipitate with barium ions, so hydrochloric acid is the correct choice here.

realWorld: Patients drink a 'barium meal' of insoluble barium sulfate before an X-ray, because barium sulfate absorbs X-rays and, being insoluble, is not absorbed into the body.
Water companies and environmental scientists test water for sulfate ions, which can come from fertilisers and mining.
Sulfate tests are used to check the composition of fertilisers such as ammonium sulfate.
separateOnlyContent: The test for sulfate ions with acidified barium chloride (part of required practical 7) is in separate Chemistry only (8462).
examTips: State the reagents in order: 'add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution'. Result: 'white precipitate'.
Do not confuse this with the halide test: sulfate uses HCl and barium chloride; halides use nitric acid and silver nitrate.
If asked why acid is added, say 'to remove carbonate ions, which would also form a white precipitate'.
Name the precipitate as barium sulfate in explanations.

questions.question: Why is dilute hydrochloric acid added before barium chloride?
options: To remove carbonate ions, which would form a white precipitate
markScheme: 1 mark: To remove carbonate ions, which would form a white precipitate
questions.explanation: Carbonate ions would form white barium carbonate; the acid removes them as carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Why must sulfuric acid NOT be used to acidify the sample?
options: It contains sulfate ions, which would always give a white precipitate
markScheme: 1 mark: It contains sulfate ions, which would always give a white precipitate
questions.explanation: Sulfuric acid adds SO₄²⁻, so a precipitate would form whatever the sample contained.

questions.question: Which is the ionic equation for the reaction in the sulfate test?
markScheme: 1 mark: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s)
questions.explanation: Barium ions are 2+ and sulfate ions 2−; only these ions form the precipitate.

questions.question: Which compound would give a white precipitate with dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride?
markScheme: 1 mark: Potassium sulfate
questions.explanation: Only potassium sulfate contains sulfate ions. Calcium carbonate's carbonate ions are removed by the acid.

Add a few drops of dilute hydrochloric acid
Purpose: removes carbonate ions, which would also form a white precipitate
Add a few drops of barium chloride solution
Purpose: provides barium ions, which form insoluble barium sulfate with sulfate ions
White precipitate shows sulfate ions

Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): barium chloride and white precipitate mentioned

questions.question: A student has four colourless solutions: sodium chloride, sodium sulfate, sodium carbonate and sodium iodide. All contain sodium ions. Describe a sequence of tests to identify each solution. Explain your choice of acids and include ionic equations for the reactions that produce precipitates or gases.
markScheme: Indicative content: flame test not useful: all give yellow (all sodium)
Add dilute acid to samples of each: only sodium carbonate fizzes; gas turns limewater milky
CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂
Sulfate test: dilute HCl then barium chloride: white precipitate only with sodium sulfate
Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄
Halide test on fresh samples: dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate
Sodium chloride: white precipitate: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl
Sodium iodide: yellow precipitate: Ag⁺ + I⁻ → AgI
Acid choice: HCl acceptable for sulfate test (Cl⁻ does not precipitate with Ba²⁺) but not for halide test (would add Cl⁻); nitric acid for halides
Never sulfuric acid in the sulfate test
Acids remove carbonate to prevent false positives
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): logical sequence identifying all four with correct results, clear explanation of acid choices and correct ionic equations
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): identifies at least three with mostly correct reagents and some explanation
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two correct tests
questions.explanation: Top answers recognise that the flame test cannot distinguish these, use the negative-ion tests in a logical order and justify each acid.
